title: Taming Spacetime Overhead and Design Complexity in Distributed Fault-Tolerant Superconducting Quantum Computation
abstract: Scaling fault-tolerant superconducting quantum computers will likely require distributed architectures built from multiple manufacturable quantum processing units. A central question is whether noisy and slow inter-chip operations impose substantial spacetime overhead or orchestration burdens compared with monolithic architectures. To answer this question, we present a hardware-grounded architectural co-design together with a comprehensive resource-estimation protocol for surface-code-based modular processors. The design confines inter-chip latency and noise to module boundaries, preventing slow, noisy links from inducing prohibitive spacetime overhead or becoming a global orchestration bottleneck. The resource-estimation protocol integrates hardware constraints and circuit-level error-correction performance into utility-scale algorithmic cost estimates, enabling a controlled assessment of different architectures. Using RSA-2048 factorization as a demanding benchmark, we estimate resources under experimentally anchored parameters and realistic superconducting hardware constraints. Compared with a large, ideal monolithic baseline, the resulting distributed architecture requires only modest additional resource overhead in both qubit count and execution time. More importantly, the overhead is nearly scale-invariant across a broad module-capacity window, decoupling chip size from global performance. This decoupling turns module capacity from a finely tuned architectural parameter into a flexible engineering degree of freedom, allowing chip sizes to be set by manufacturability and control-packaging constraints rather than architectural fine-tuning. These results establish a viable route to distributed fault-tolerant superconducting quantum computation that scales without prohibitive resource growth or heavy orchestration burden.
summary: This paper analyzes the feasibility of scaling fault-tolerant quantum computation using distributed superconducting architectures. By developing a rigorous resource estimation protocol, the authors demonstrate that inter-chip communication overhead does not lead to prohibitive resource growth. This establishes a viable, scalable pathway for building large quantum computers constrained by manufacturability.
main_problem: The paper addresses whether the overhead introduced by distributing fault-tolerant quantum computation across multiple, physically separated quantum processing units (QPUs) is prohibitive compared to monolithic designs.
main_result: The proposed distributed architecture shows only a modest, nearly scale-invariant resource overhead in both qubit count and execution time compared to ideal monolithic baselines.
method: The authors developed a hardware-grounded architectural co-design and a comprehensive resource-estimation protocol that integrates physical hardware constraints and circuit-level error-correction performance.
model_or_system: The work focuses on superconducting quantum computers utilizing surface-code-based modular processors, where computation is partitioned across multiple interconnected chips.
key_observables: Spacetime overhead (qubit count and execution time) for factoring large integers like RSA-2048.
important_parameters: Inter-chip latency/noise factors ($\eta$, $\gamma$), module capacity, and physical error rates ($p$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes nearest-neighbor connectivity and relies on specific hardware parameters for superconducting qubits.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the spacetime overhead comparison between monolithic and distributed architectures (Fig. 1), and detail the multi-layered procedure for resource estimation in the DFTQC architecture (Fig. 2).
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem of modular overhead, presents a resource estimation protocol, applies it to a demanding benchmark (RSA-2048), and demonstrates that the overhead is manageable and scale-invariant.
why_interesting: While focused on superconducting hardware, the core concepts of resource scaling, overhead analysis, and architectural decoupling are highly relevant to any physical platform (like trapped ions or superconducting circuits) aiming for large-scale fault tolerance.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks
